VBO:0200004.summary: The Afghan Hound comes from Afghanistan’s mountains, where a fast, powerful sighthound pursued game across difficult ground. Its proud carriage, long silky coat and distinctive topknot can make the athletic frame beneath look almost theatrical.
VBO:0200004.interestingFact: An Afghan named Zardin drew attention at London’s Crystal Palace show in 1907, soon after the first examples reached Britain.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 228: Afghan Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Afghan mountain origins, hunting use, the long silky coat and topknot, and Zardin’s 1907 show appearance.

VBO:0200008.summary: The Airedale is Yorkshire’s largest terrier, named for the Aire valley’s waterside dogs. Its wiry black-and-tan coat and sturdy working build suited a breed used for tracking and, later, police and wartime service across several countries.
VBO:0200008.interestingFact: The breed’s “King of Terriers” nickname reflects its size: the FCI describes it as the largest terrier.
VBO:0200008.historicalRoots: Yorkshire waterside terrier developed for versatile work.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 7: Airedale Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard places the breed in Yorkshire’s Aire river valleys, describes size and wiry coat, and records tracking, Red Cross, police and military work.

VBO:0200016.summary: Developed in Alaska by Linda Spurlin’s family, the Alaskan Klee Kai keeps the wedge head, upright ears and double coat of a northern spitz in a much smaller frame. A sharply contrasting facial mask is its signature, while the well-furred tail curls over the back when alert.
VBO:0200016.interestingFact: The UKC recognizes toy, miniature and standard height varieties, all within a companion-sized northern breed.
VBO:0200016.historicalRoots: Alaskan companion breed developed from northern spitz-type dogs in the 1970s and 1980s.

sources.title: UKC Alaskan Klee Kai breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard names Linda Spurlin, Alaskan development, northern ancestry, three size varieties, facial mask and curled tail.

VBO:0200034.summary: The American Bulldog carries forward a working bulldog tradition preserved on Southern farms after its older type disappeared from Britain. Bred to catch hogs and cattle and guard property, it has a powerful frame, broad head and a range of athletic to heavier-built lines.
VBO:0200034.interestingFact: Postwar breeders John D. Johnson and Alan Scott helped rebuild the breed; their lines remain part of its history.
VBO:0200034.historicalRoots: Southern U.S. farm and stock-working bulldog.

sources.title: UKC American Bulldog breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard covers Southern farm use, cattle and hog catching, Johnson and Scott recovery work, broad head and variation among working lines.

VBO:0200047.summary: The American Foxhound is a long-legged American scent hound built to travel with a pack on a fox trail. Its deep chest, straight running legs and long, low-set ears give the outline of a dog bred for sustained movement rather than a brief sprint.
VBO:0200047.interestingFact: The FCI places the American Foxhound among large scent hounds and specifies a working trial.
VBO:0200047.historicalRoots: American pack hound developed for fox hunting.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 303: American Foxhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard classifies it as a large scent hound with a working trial and describes chest, legs and ears.

sources.title: AKC: What Hound Group Dogs Were Bred to Do
sources.evidence: Identifies American Foxhound fox-hunting use and emphasis on speed and endurance.

VBO:0200059.summary: The American Water Spaniel was shaped for American waterways: a medium-sized hunting dog able to retrieve from a skiff or canoe and work on land. Its dense marcel-to-curly coat and balanced, muscular build suit a compact all-around gun dog.
VBO:0200059.interestingFact: Unlike many larger retrievers, its standard explicitly calls out retrieving from small boats.
VBO:0200059.historicalRoots: U.S. waterfowl and upland hunting dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 301: American Water Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard states U.S. origin, skiff/canoe retrieving, land work, medium muscular size and marcel-to-curly coat.

VBO:0200077.summary: The Armenian Gampr is a livestock guardian landrace from the Armenian Highlands, shaped by generations of work with flocks and homesteads. It commonly has a strong, slightly long body and a weather-ready coat, while coat length and overall appearance vary across working populations.
VBO:0200077.interestingFact: The Gampr club treats it as a landrace with a descriptive breed account, preserving working variation rather than one rigid outline.
VBO:0200077.historicalRoots: Armenian Highlands livestock and homestead guardian.

sources.title: Armenian Gampr Club breed description
sources.evidence: Armenian Gampr Club describes the highland origin, guardian use, landrace status, strong slightly long build and variable coat.

VBO:0200097.summary: The Australian Stumpy Tail Cattle Dog was developed for moving cattle through Australia’s rough, open country. Its naturally short tail, upright ears and spare, sturdy outline distinguish it from the better-known Australian Cattle Dog, while its history centers on practical droving work.
VBO:0200097.interestingFact: The FCI history notes competing accounts of the breed’s early crosses, so no single origin story is certain.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 351: Australian Stumpy Tail Cattle Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Australian cattle work, naturally short tail, erect ears and differing accounts of early development.

VBO:0200103.summary: The Austrian Pinscher descends from Austrian country pinschers once common as versatile farm dogs. More substantial than a toy pinscher, it has a compact, lively outline, short dense coat and an alert farmyard bearing that fits its watchdog and small-farm roots.
VBO:0200103.interestingFact: Systematic breeding began in 1921; the breed’s name changed from Austrian Shorthaired Pinscher in 2000.
VBO:0200103.historicalRoots: Austrian farm dog refined through twentieth-century breeding.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 64: Austrian Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces country-pinscher farm origins, describes build and coat, and dates organized breeding and the 2000 name change.

VBO:0200121.summary: The Basque Shepherd Dog is a herding dog of Spain’s Basque country, built for steady work over open ground. Its Iletsua variety has an elongated, strong body and a bristly blond-to-cinnamon coat; the distinct Gorbeiakoa variety is redder and somewhat shorter in proportion.
VBO:0200121.interestingFact: The RSCE publishes separate Iletsua and Gorbeiakoa standards under the Basque Shepherd Dog name.
VBO:0200121.historicalRoots: Basque livestock herding dog with Iletsua and Gorbeiakoa varieties.

sources.title: RSCE Basque Shepherd Dog, Iletsua standard
sources.evidence: Spanish Royal Canine Society Iletsua standard identifies Basque herding use, rectangular proportions and bristly blond/fawn/cinnamon coat; the society recognizes both varieties.

sources.title: RSCE Basque Shepherd Dog, Gorbeiakoa standard
sources.evidence: Confirms related breed variety or history described in the summary.

VBO:0200126.summary: The Basset Hound pairs a ground-hugging body with the nose and stamina of a scent hound. French basset roots were developed further in Britain; the breed was made to follow hare at a deliberate pace through heavy cover and over long distances.
VBO:0200126.interestingFact: Its low station keeps the nose close to the scent trail, a functional feature rather than a novelty.
VBO:0200126.historicalRoots: French basset hunting roots; developed further in Britain for hare trailing.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 163: Basset Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard records French monastic tradition, British development, hare hunting over distance and low scenting build.

VBO:0200136.summary: The Beauceron is a large French sheepdog of the plains, bred to move and guard flocks. A short, harsh coat, strong frame and tan markings on the lower legs give this working dog the old French nickname Bas Rouge, or “red stockings.”
VBO:0200136.interestingFact: Its paired hind dewclaws are a distinctive requirement of the breed standard.
VBO:0200136.historicalRoots: French plains sheepdog selected for flock driving and guarding.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 44: Beauceron
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes French plains herding origin, black-and-tan markings, short harsh coat and double hind dewclaws.

VBO:0200158.summary: The Berger Picard is a rough-coated French herder associated with Picardy and the wider northwest European sheepdog tradition. Its tall ears, tousled coat and lean rectangular build preserve a practical pastoral look; fanciers searched Picardy for typical dogs after World War II.
VBO:0200158.interestingFact: The FCI account traces a postwar revival before the modern breed club gained recognition in 1959.
VBO:0200158.historicalRoots: French rough-coated sheep and cattle herder, revived after World War II.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 176: Berger Picard
sources.evidence: FCI standard discusses Picardy association, rough-coated herding type, postwar search and 1959 club recognition; appearance section covers coat and ears.

VBO:0200168.summary: The Black and Tan Coonhound is an American trail-and-tree hound that follows raccoon scent across difficult ground. Its long ears, deep voice and glossy black coat with tan markings belong to a dog bred for endurance through both summer heat and winter cold.
VBO:0200168.interestingFact: The standard stresses that it tracks entirely by scent before treeing its quarry.
VBO:0200168.historicalRoots: American scent hound developed for raccoon trailing and treeing.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 300: Black and Tan Coonhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard defines raccoon scent-trailing and treeing, all-weather working conditions, long ears and black-and-tan coat.

VBO:0200186.summary: The Bohemian Shepherd Dog, or Chodský pes, is a Czech herder with a long black-and-tan coat and compact, sturdy shape. Historic accounts from the Chodsko region describe long-coated dogs used for guarding and cattle work, while the modern breed preserves a similarly practical pastoral outline.
VBO:0200186.interestingFact: A dog silhouette appeared on the Chodsko people’s pennon, according to the breed’s historical account.
VBO:0200186.historicalRoots: Czech herding and homestead-guarding tradition associated with Chodsko.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 364: Bohemian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Chodsko historical references with explicit pedigree caution, guarding/cattle work, coat and build.

VBO:0200194.summary: The Border Terrier was made for the English-Scottish border country, where a working terrier needed enough leg to follow a horse and enough grit for earth work. Its narrow body, wiry coat and characteristic “otter” head keep the small dog firmly in the practical terrier tradition.
VBO:0200194.interestingFact: The FCI standard’s compact test of type is simple: a working terrier capable of following a horse.
VBO:0200194.historicalRoots: Border-country working terrier for mounted hunts and earth work.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 10: Border Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard specifies horse-following working utility, narrow build, wiry coat and otter-like head; origin is Great Britain.

sources.title: AKC: Border Terrier facts
sources.evidence: Places development along the England–Scotland border and describes work with mounted hunts and underground quarry.

VBO:0200208.summary: The Bouvier des Flandres grew from local stock-driving dogs on both the Belgian and French sides of Flanders. Its broad, powerful body and harsh, shaggy coat reflect the demands of moving cattle; the beard gives the working silhouette a memorable face.
VBO:0200208.interestingFact: The FCI standard treats Flanders as a shared region, not a breed confined to one side of a modern border.
VBO:0200208.historicalRoots: Flanders cattle drover from Belgian and French farming communities.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 191: Bouvier des Flandres
sources.evidence: FCI standard explicitly locates origin on both sides of Flanders, recounts drovers selecting local dogs, and describes sturdy shaggy conformation.

VBO:0200215.summary: The Bracco Italiano is an old Italian bird dog whose long ears, sculpted head and strong, fluid trot set it apart from other pointers. The breed’s history stretches back to fourteenth-century images, while its field role joins pointing with retrieving.
VBO:0200215.interestingFact: Its official standard prizes a fast, wide trot as well as the ability to retrieve.
VBO:0200215.historicalRoots: Italian bird-hunting pointer with longstanding field tradition.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 202: Bracco Italiano
sources.evidence: FCI standard cites fourteenth-century frescoes, bird hunting, pointing, retrieving and wide trot; appearance describes ears and head.

VBO:0200238.summary: The Brittany comes from France’s Brittany region, where a compact bird dog was developed for pointing work. Its lively, balanced frame and naturally short or absent tail suit a close-working field companion; a breed standard was adopted in 1908.
VBO:0200238.interestingFact: The first club standard was presented at Loudéac in June 1908 under a name emphasizing the natural short tail.
VBO:0200238.historicalRoots: French Brittany pointing dog; formal standard adopted in 1908.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 95: Brittany
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Brittany origin, pointing use, natural short tail and 1908 club standard.

VBO:0200261.summary: The Bullmastiff combines mastiff substance with bulldog ancestry in a powerful British guard dog. Gamekeepers once used it to help apprehend poachers; the short coat, broad head and strong, compact body still convey that practical history.
VBO:0200261.interestingFact: Its gamekeeper role was to stop and hold an intruder, not to range ahead as a hunting hound.
VBO:0200261.historicalRoots: British gamekeeper’s guard dog developed from mastiff and bulldog stock.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 157: Bullmastiff
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Old English Mastiff and Bulldog ancestry, gamekeeper use against poachers and broad powerful build.

VBO:0200271.summary: The Campeiro Bulldog is a Brazilian stock-working bulldog developed in the south of the country from dogs brought by European immigrants. Its broad head and compact, muscular body served cattle catching and driving on farms and in native scrub; the name Campeiro points to its rural setting.
VBO:0200271.interestingFact: Brazil’s breed standard also records its former use holding cattle in old slaughterhouses.
VBO:0200271.historicalRoots: Southern Brazilian cattle-catching and farm-guarding bulldog.

sources.title: CBKC Brazilian Campeiro Bulldog standard
sources.evidence: Brazilian CBKC standard traces European immigrant bulldogs, southern cattle work and slaughterhouse history; appearance describes medium, compact muscular build.

VBO:0200290.summary: The Cardigan Welsh Corgi is a low, long-bodied Welsh cattle dog with enough toughness and mobility for herding work. Its fox-like brush tail extends the line of the body, giving the Cardigan a different silhouette from the shorter-tailed Pembroke.
VBO:0200290.interestingFact: Its long body and brush tail are central to the Cardigan silhouette.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 38: Cardigan Welsh Corgi
sources.evidence: FCI standard lists herding use and describes sturdy mobile body, long proportions and fox-like brush tail.

VBO:0200309.summary: The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel is a small British companion spaniel with a gently rounded expression, long feathered ears and a silky coat. Its balanced, active outline preserves a sporting note beneath the toy-dog scale.
VBO:0200309.interestingFact: Its four accepted color patterns include Blenheim, tricolor, ruby and black-and-tan.
VBO:0200309.historicalRoots: British toy spaniel developed as a companion.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 136: Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard lists companion/toy role, balanced active appearance, long feathered ears and four colors.

VBO:0200326.summary: The Chesapeake Bay Retriever was developed on the Chesapeake to fetch waterfowl in wind, tide and icy water. A strong frame and short, oily, wavy double coat help this American retriever handle long cold swims and repeated retrieves.
VBO:0200326.interestingFact: The standard specifically anticipates breaking ice during waterfowl work.
VBO:0200326.historicalRoots: Chesapeake Bay waterfowl retriever bred for severe conditions.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 263: Chesapeake Bay Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard details Chesapeake origin, adverse waterfowl work including ice, powerful body and oily wavy double coat.

VBO:0200353.summary: The Chinook began with a single tawny sled dog born on Arthur Walden’s New Hampshire farm in 1917. Bred to blend freight-dog strength with racing-dog speed, the modern Chinook has a substantial, athletic body, double coat and low-set saber tail.
VBO:0200353.interestingFact: The original Chinook accompanied Admiral Byrd’s first Antarctic expedition with Arthur Walden’s sled-dog team.
VBO:0200353.historicalRoots: New Hampshire sled dog developed in the early twentieth century.

sources.title: UKC Chinook breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard identifies Walden’s 1917 foundation dog, freight/racing aims, Byrd expedition participation and tawny double-coated form.

VBO:0200364.summary: The Cimarrón Uruguayo is a sturdy Uruguayan dog descended from animals introduced during the colonial era. After generations of free-ranging survival, people brought these dogs into estate guarding and cattle work; the modern outline is muscular and agile rather than ponderous.
VBO:0200364.interestingFact: Its standard is frank that the exact early origin is uncertain.
VBO:0200364.historicalRoots: Uruguayan cattle and estate guardian descended from introduced colonial dogs.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 353: Cimarron Uruguayo
sources.evidence: FCI standard states uncertain origin, colonial dog ancestry, natural selection and later guarding/herding use, with compact muscular appearance.

VBO:0200392.summary: The Croatian Sheepdog is a compact, agile black herder rooted in eastern Slavonia. A lightly waved or curled coat, pointed ears and quick-footed build suit the livestock work that shaped it; organized breeding began in the 1930s.
VBO:0200392.interestingFact: The breed was publicly presented at a Zagreb dog show in 1949.
VBO:0200392.historicalRoots: Eastern Slavonian livestock herder; systematic breeding from 1935.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 277: Croatian Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents eastern Slavonian history, 1935 breeding and 1949 show; appearance details black curled coat and ears.

VBO:0200427.summary: The Dalmatian’s spotted white coat is unmistakable, while its history links it to Croatia’s Dalmatian region and the old coach-dog tradition. Regional paintings and church records show spotted hounds there from the early seventeenth century.
VBO:0200427.interestingFact: A Croatian church painting dated around 1600–1630 is among the early visual records cited by the FCI.
VBO:0200427.historicalRoots: Croatian Dalmatian-region hound with later coach-dog history.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 153: Dalmatian
sources.evidence: FCI standard cites Croatian paintings and church records, Dalmatian name and spotted coat; historical section notes coach-dog designation.

VBO:0200442.summary: The Doberman Pinscher takes its name from Friedrich Louis Dobermann, who developed a protective working dog in nineteenth-century Germany. Its clean, square outline, short coat and black-or-brown markings give a sharp silhouette shaped by guard and police work.
VBO:0200442.interestingFact: Early police use earned the breed the German nickname “Gendarme dog.”
VBO:0200442.historicalRoots: German protective working dog developed by Friedrich Louis Dobermann.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 143: Doberman Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard names the founder, nineteenth-century development, guard and police use, square build and coat colors.

VBO:0200450.summary: The Dogue de Bordeaux is a powerful French mastiff long associated with Aquitaine. Its massive head, broad chest and short fawn coat recall a past that included guarding houses and cattle and hunting large game; the breed nearly vanished after the world wars.
VBO:0200450.interestingFact: The first French dog show in 1863 listed these dogs under the Dogue de Bordeaux name.
VBO:0200450.historicalRoots: French molosser of Aquitaine, historically a guard and big-game dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 116: Dogue de Bordeaux
sources.evidence: FCI standard records Aquitaine, guarding and hunting uses, 1863 show and postwar decline; appearance describes head, chest and fawn coat.

VBO:0200456.summary: The Dunker, also called the Norwegian Hound, is a hare scent hound created by Wilhelm Conrad Dunker in nineteenth-century Norway. Its athletic build and long ears fit a working hound; a striking blue-marbled coat with light eyes is characteristic, though other colors are permitted.
VBO:0200456.interestingFact: The FCI account notes later controlled outcrossing to improve genetic variety in a small population.
VBO:0200456.historicalRoots: Norwegian hare hound developed by Wilhelm Conrad Dunker.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 203: Dunker
sources.evidence: FCI standard names creator, hare hunting, blue-marbled coat and eye variation, and documents outcrossing for diversity.

VBO:0200490.summary: The English Foxhound is a purpose-built pack hound, with a strong, balanced body and endurance for long days following fox scent. Its breeding was recorded by English hunt masters for more than two centuries, leaving unusually deep studbook trails.
VBO:0200490.interestingFact: Masters of Foxhounds Association studbooks reach back before 1800.
VBO:0200490.historicalRoots: English pack hound with documented fox-hunting lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 159: English Foxhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes foxhound breeding by English hunt masters, early studbooks, pack history and strong hound conformation.

VBO:0200502.summary: The Entlebuch Cattle Dog is the smallest of Switzerland’s four mountain and cattle dog breeds, named for a valley around Lucerne and Bern. Its compact, agile frame and black, white and tan coat belong to a farm dog once used to drive stock and watch the holding.
VBO:0200502.interestingFact: The breed was not clearly separated from the Appenzeller in early records; its own standard followed in 1927.
VBO:0200502.historicalRoots: Swiss Entlebuch valley stock driver and farm guard.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 47: Entlebuch Cattle Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Entlebuch origin, smallest Swiss mountain-dog status, driving/watch work and 1927 standard; appearance describes tricolor build.

VBO:0200512.summary: The Eurasier is a German companion spitz created in the 1960s from Chow Chow and Wolfspitz lines, with Samoyed added later. A medium frame, dense double coat, upright ears and curled tail give it a classic northern outline without a hunting or herding job behind its name.
VBO:0200512.interestingFact: It was first called the Wolf-Chow before the Samoyed cross and Eurasier name.
VBO:0200512.historicalRoots: German companion spitz founded by Julius Wipfel in the 1960s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 291: Eurasier
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Wipfel, founding crosses, former Wolf-Chow name and companion use; appearance describes coat, ears and tail.

VBO:0200523.summary: The Finnish Lapphund grew from the reindeer-herding dogs used by Sámi communities across northern Fennoscandia. Its profuse weatherproof coat, upright ears and mobile, medium-sized body suit cold-country work; today it is also widely kept as a companion in Finland.
VBO:0200523.interestingFact: The breed’s English name changed more than once as Finnish registries separated related Lapponian types.
VBO:0200523.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding tradition in northern Fennoscandia.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 189: Finnish Lapphund
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Sámi reindeer work, Finnish name changes and companion use; appearance details coat, ears and medium size.

VBO:0201455.summary: The French Bulldog took shape in the working neighborhoods of Paris in the 1880s. Compact and muscular, with a short coat and upright bat ears, it moved from the circles of porters, butchers and coachmen into Parisian social and artistic life.
VBO:0201455.interestingFact: The first breed club was founded in Paris in 1880, with the first registration recorded in 1885.
VBO:0201455.historicalRoots: Parisian companion dog developed in the late nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 101: French Bulldog
sources.evidence: FCI standard dates Paris development, working-class ownership, later popularity and club founding; appearance describes compact build and bat ears.

VBO:0200563.summary: The Georgian Shepherd, or Kartuli Nagazi, is a large, strong guardian from Georgia’s mountain regions. A slightly long body, short coat with a dense undercoat and steady protective work mark this regional dog, whose appearance has been shaped by mountain conditions.
VBO:0200563.interestingFact: Georgia’s cynological federation issued a national standard for the Georgian mountain dog in 2000, while international recognition remained separate.
VBO:0200563.historicalRoots: Georgian mountain guardian and pastoral dog.

sources.title: Elkana Georgian agricultural biodiversity: Georgian Shepherd
sources.evidence: Elkana Georgian agricultural biodiversity account identifies Georgian mountain origin, Nagazi identity, guardian role, short dense coat, body proportions and 2000 national standard.

VBO:0200583.summary: The German Shorthaired Pointer became a versatile gundog as older European pointing lines were refined in Germany. It can point, track and retrieve, with a lean, powerful frame and close coat suited to moving steadily from field to water.
VBO:0200583.interestingFact: The Deutsch-Kurzhaar studbook began publication in 1897 as a foundation for organized breeding and trials.
VBO:0200583.historicalRoots: German all-purpose pointing dog refined from European bird-hunting lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 119: German Shorthaired Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI standard explains European pointing roots, versatile gundog selection, 1897 studbook and athletic short-coated build.

VBO:0200609.summary: The Glen of Imaal Terrier comes from a remote Irish valley where a small, sturdy dog had to earn its keep. Its low, powerful body and rough coat served practical farm work before the breed became a show-ring fixture; the Irish Kennel Club recognized it in 1934.
VBO:0200609.interestingFact: The FCI history records that Glen terriers once worked dog-powered wheels, a vanished farm practice.
VBO:0200609.historicalRoots: Irish Glen of Imaal farm terrier selected for hard local work.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 302: Glen of Imaal Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes the Glen’s Irish locality, farm work, dog-wheel history, sturdy rough-coated build and 1934 recognition.

VBO:0200629.summary: The Great Pyrenees is the Pyrenean Mountain Dog: a large white guardian shaped by centuries in the mountains between France and Spain. Its substantial frame and heavy weather-resistant coat suited watching flocks, while the breed later appeared at French castles and royal court.
VBO:0200629.interestingFact: The breed’s presence at Louis XIV’s court followed an older mountain and castle-guarding history.
VBO:0200629.historicalRoots: Pyrenean flock guardian with medieval castle associations.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 137: Great Pyrenees
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Pyrenean guardian history, castles and Louis XIV’s court; appearance describes large white weather-resistant coat.

VBO:0200638.summary: The Greyhound is the classic British sighthound, built for visual pursuit with a deep chest, long legs and supple, aerodynamic frame. Coursing hare shaped the type before organized racing, making speed central to its identity without erasing its older hunting history.
VBO:0200638.interestingFact: The FCI history cites a racing Greyhound clocked above 45 miles per hour.
VBO:0200638.historicalRoots: British-developed hare-coursing sighthound later used in racing.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 158: Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies British development, hare coursing, racing and speed, with deep-chested athletic build.

VBO:0200667.summary: The Hellenic Hound is a Greek scent hound built to follow a trail over broken terrain. Its lean, muscular outline, hanging ears and short black-and-tan coat form a distinct working silhouette, with stamina and a resonant voice suited to rough mountain ground.
VBO:0200667.interestingFact: Its standard places it among medium-sized scent hounds with a working trial.
VBO:0200667.historicalRoots: Greek scent hound traditionally worked over varied, rocky terrain.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 214: Hellenic Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Greek origin, medium scent-hound classification, all-terrain hunting use, resonant voice and black-and-tan athletic build.

VBO:0200678.summary: The Hungarian Greyhound, or Magyar Agár, is a robust sighthound tied to hunting traditions in Hungary. More substantial than many racing silhouettes, it combines a deep chest and strong legs with the speed for coursing; nineteenth-century crossings sought still greater pace.
VBO:0200678.interestingFact: The FCI history links the type to the Magyar settlement of Hungary and records later sighthound crosses.
VBO:0200678.historicalRoots: Hungarian hunting sighthound with medieval roots and nineteenth-century refinement.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 240: Hungarian Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Magyar Agár, hunting roots and nineteenth-century speed crosses; appearance describes strong deep-chested build.

VBO:0200692.summary: The Icelandic Sheepdog descends from dogs brought by Iceland’s Viking settlers and became essential to farm stock work. This lively spitz has upright ears, a curled tail and a thick coat suited to wind and weather, with a working style shaped by Icelandic terrain.
VBO:0200692.interestingFact: The FCI dates the settlers’ arrival to roughly AD 870–930.
VBO:0200692.historicalRoots: Icelandic farm and livestock dog descending from settler dogs.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 289: Icelandic Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Viking-settler history, livestock work, climate and spitz appearance.

VBO:0200702.summary: The Irish Setter began as a red working bird dog, selected in Ireland for hunting game with stamina and style. A lean head, flowing chestnut coat and feathered tail give the breed its famous sweep, but its history is firmly rooted in field work.
VBO:0200702.interestingFact: The Irish Red Setter Club issued a breed standard in 1886 and has long paired shows with field trials.
VBO:0200702.historicalRoots: Irish red setter developed for bird hunting.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 120: Irish Setter
sources.evidence: FCI standard details Irish hunting origin, club and 1886 standard, field trials, chestnut coat and feathering.

VBO:0200709.summary: The Istrian Short-Haired Hound is a white-and-orange scent hound of Croatia’s Adriatic region, traditionally used for hare and fox. Its clean, short coat and fine, strong frame give an agile outline; regional art and written records document hound types there for centuries.
VBO:0200709.interestingFact: A fourteenth-century Dubrovnik monastery carving is among the early records cited in its standard.
VBO:0200709.historicalRoots: Croatian Adriatic hare and fox scent hound.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 151: Istrian Short-Haired Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes East Adriatic hound roots, medieval art evidence, hare/fox use and white coat with orange markings.

VBO:0200721.summary: The Italian Spinone is a rugged Italian pointing dog with a wiry coat, heavy brows and a memorable beard. Its broad, steady trot and patient field style suit rough cover; references to similar rough-haired Italian dogs appear in old hunting writing and art.
VBO:0200721.interestingFact: The FCI cites a fifteenth-century Mantua fresco among depictions of the breed’s ancestors.
VBO:0200721.historicalRoots: Italian rough-haired pointing dog with longstanding field use.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 165: Italian Spinone
sources.evidence: FCI standard covers Italian rough-haired history, Mantua painting, pointing use, trot, wiry coat and beard.

VBO:0200733.summary: The Jämthund is a large Swedish hunting spitz, long present in the north but recognized separately only in 1946. Its gray coat, erect ears and strong curled tail frame a dog used chiefly to find and bay elk, with endurance for lengthy work in forest country.
VBO:0200733.interestingFact: It was once judged together with the smaller Norwegian Elkhound before separate recognition.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 42: Jämthund
sources.evidence: FCI standard records 1946 recognition, prior grouping with Norwegian Elkhound, elk-baying work and gray spitz appearance.

VBO:0200741.summary: The Japanese Terrier is a small, smooth-coated dog developed from imported fox terriers and local small dogs in Japan’s port cities. Its dark head and mostly white body make a crisp silhouette; it served mainly as a lapdog in Kobe and Yokohama before organized breeding fixed the type.
VBO:0200741.interestingFact: The FCI traces imported smooth fox terriers to Nagasaki trade with the Netherlands in the seventeenth century.
VBO:0200741.historicalRoots: Japanese port-city companion terrier refined in the early twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 259: Japanese Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Dutch-imported terrier roots, port-city lapdog use, early twentieth-century breeding and characteristic coat.

VBO:0200751.summary: The Kanni is a lean southern Indian hound whose long legs, deep chest and tucked abdomen fit a fast visual hunter. Its breeding tract lies in Tamil Nadu’s Virudhunagar, Tuticorin and Tirunelveli districts; observed coats include black-and-tan, tan, cream and fawn.
VBO:0200751.interestingFact: A morphometric study documented regional variation rather than one universally fixed coat color.
VBO:0200751.historicalRoots: Tamil Nadu indigenous hound associated with hunting and companionship.

sources.title: Selvakkumar et al., Morphometric Characterization of Kanni Dog
sources.evidence: Indian Veterinary Journal field study identifies Kanni’s southern Tamil Nadu breeding tract, hunting use, slim build, deep chest and observed coat colors.

VBO:0200759.summary: The Keeshond is a Dutch spitz once familiar on canal barges as a watchful companion. Its stand-off gray-and-black double coat, curled plume and dark facial “spectacles” give it one of the most recognizable expressions among northern dogs.
VBO:0200759.interestingFact: The breed became a symbol of the Dutch Patriot movement, with its name linked to the leader Kees.
VBO:0200759.historicalRoots: Dutch barge companion and watchdog with spitz ancestry.

sources.title: UKC Keeshond breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard recounts barge use, Patriot association, spitz ancestry and signature coat, plume and spectacle markings.

VBO:0200774.summary: The Kishu Ken is a Japanese mountain hunting dog from the Kishu region, especially associated with wild boar. Its medium spitz frame, upright ears and curled or sickle tail suit a nimble hunter; today’s solid-colored coats followed an earlier period with more visible markings.
VBO:0200774.interestingFact: Japan designated the breed a natural monument in 1934, the year solid colors became the accepted standard.
VBO:0200774.historicalRoots: Kishu mountain hunter used mainly for wild boar.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 318: Kishu Ken
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Kishu region, boar hunting, earlier marked coats and 1934 natural-monument designation; appearance covers ears and tail.

VBO:0200786.summary: The Kromfohrländer is a relatively recent German companion breed named for the Krom Fohr district near Siegen. Developed from wire-haired Fox Terrier and Grand Griffon Vendéen ancestry, it comes in rough and smooth coats, typically white with brown patches.
VBO:0200786.interestingFact: International recognition arrived in 1955, only a short time after the breed’s founding.
VBO:0200786.historicalRoots: German companion breed developed near Siegen in the mid-twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 192: Kromfohrlander
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Krom Fohr name, founder, two ancestral breeds and 1955 recognition; coat section distinguishes varieties.

VBO:0200814.summary: The Lapponian Herder is a Finnish reindeer worker from the long Sámi pastoral tradition. Its close-fitting double coat, upright ears and long, low-carried tail distinguish this steady trotter from the more profusely coated Finnish Lapphund.
VBO:0200814.interestingFact: The two modern Lapponian breeds were separated in Finnish registry practice in 1966.
VBO:0200814.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding dog of northern Finland.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 284: Lapponian Herder
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Sámi reindeer work and 1966 separation; appearance describes coat, ears, tail and trotting form.

VBO:0200824.summary: The Lhasa Apso comes from high-altitude Tibet, where a small dog needed a dense, hard coat against wind, dust and cold. Its long hair and fall over the eyes are functional as well as striking; Britain first received examples in the early 1920s.
VBO:0200824.interestingFact: Early British fanciers grouped it with other shaggy Tibetan dogs under the loose name “Lhasa Terrier.”
VBO:0200824.historicalRoots: Tibetan highland companion; introduced to Britain in the 1920s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 227: Lhasa Apso
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Tibetan altitude and coat function, British arrival and early Lhasa Terrier naming.

VBO:0200862.summary: The Manchester Terrier is a sleek black-and-tan English ratter whose name points to the city where it became a recognized show type. Its narrow head, close coat and swift outline recall nineteenth-century vermin control rather than a purely decorative terrier.
VBO:0200862.interestingFact: Manchester pub shows in the mid-1800s helped the terrier gain classes of its own.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 71: Manchester Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents ratting, Manchester pub shows and name, with sleek black-and-tan appearance.

VBO:0200893.summary: The Miniature Pinscher is a small German pinscher with a compact square frame, smooth coat and brisk, ground-covering trot. Although its outline can suggest a tiny Doberman, the breed has its own pinscher history and was already numerous in German studbooks by the early twentieth century.
VBO:0200893.interestingFact: The 1925 German studbook recorded more than 1,300 Miniature Pinschers.
VBO:0200893.historicalRoots: German small pinscher established before the twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 185: Miniature Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents 1925 studbook total, square frame, smooth red or black-and-tan coat and ground-covering trot.

VBO:0200920.summary: The Mudhol Hound is a lean Indian sighthound associated with northern Karnataka and the western Deccan. Its long, narrow head, deep chest and strongly tucked abdomen suit swift pursuit across open country, while local breeders preserve both smooth and silky-coated forms.
VBO:0200920.interestingFact: University researchers measured 150 Mudhol Hounds in Bagalkot-area villages to document the regional type.
VBO:0200920.historicalRoots: Karnataka sighthound of the western Deccan.

sources.title: Dodamani et al., Physical and Performance Characteristics of Mudhol Hound Dogs
sources.evidence: University field study identifies northern Karnataka home tract, sighthound use, narrow head, deep chest, tucked abdomen and two coat varieties; it measured 150 dogs.

VBO:0200932.summary: The Nederlandse Kooikerhondje is a small Dutch decoy dog with orange-red patches, feathered ears and a waving white-plumed tail. Working among reed screens, it draws curious ducks down a decoy pipe rather than retrieving them; the modern breed was rebuilt during World War II.
VBO:0200932.interestingFact: A Friesland farm bitch named Tommy became the foundation dog in Baroness van Hardenbroek’s revival.
VBO:0200932.historicalRoots: Dutch duck-decoy worker revived in the 1940s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 314: Nederlandse Kooikerhondje
sources.evidence: FCI standard explains decoy-pipe work, 1942 revival and Tommy foundation bitch; appearance describes orange-white coat and plume.

VBO:0200953.summary: The Norwegian Buhund is a square-built farm spitz with upright ears, a curled tail and a dense coat. Norway’s farmers used it for both herding and watch work, and the breed type appears in accounts reaching back toward the Viking Age.
VBO:0200953.interestingFact: The Norwegian word buhund means “farmstead dog.”
VBO:0200953.historicalRoots: Norwegian farm, herding and watch dog with old spitz roots.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 237: Norwegian Buhund
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces farm work, Viking-era evidence, name meaning and square spitz appearance.

VBO:0200964.summary: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever was developed on Canada’s Atlantic coast to lure waterfowl toward hunters and then retrieve them. Smaller than many retrievers, it has an alert red-orange coat, feathered tail and energetic shoreline working style.
VBO:0200964.interestingFact: “Tolling” names the lure phase of the hunt, before the dog retrieves the downed birds.
VBO:0200964.historicalRoots: Nova Scotian waterfowl tolling and retrieving dog of the nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 312: Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Nova Scotia development, early nineteenth-century tolling/retrieving use, red coat and feathered tail.

VBO:0200980.summary: The Otterhound is a large British scent hound built for following otter scent over land and through water. Its rough, oily coat, broad feet and resonant bay speak to that demanding former work; otter hunting is now banned in Britain.
VBO:0200980.interestingFact: Houndsmen called a land scent trail a “drag” and a waterborne one a “wash.”
VBO:0200980.historicalRoots: British otter-trailing scent hound, a former hunting role.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 294: Otterhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes otter work and its ban, drag/wash terms, oily coat, webbed feet and baying call.

VBO:0200995.summary: The Pembroke Welsh Corgi is a low, sturdy Welsh cattle dog with a foxlike head, upright ears and a surprising amount of working stamina in a small frame. Its shorter tail tradition and lighter outline help distinguish it from the longer, brush-tailed Cardigan.
VBO:0200995.interestingFact: The standard permits a natural short tail; tail length alone cannot identify every Pembroke.
VBO:0200995.historicalRoots: Welsh cattle herder with a compact low build.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 39: Pembroke Welsh Corgi
sources.evidence: FCI standard lists cattledog use, low sturdy form, foxlike head, prick ears and natural short-tail provision.

VBO:0201032.summary: The Polish Greyhound, or Chart Polski, is a powerful Polish sighthound recorded in hunting art and writing from the thirteenth century onward. Its deep chest, strong limbs and more substantial build than many sighthounds match a history of open-country pursuit.
VBO:0201032.interestingFact: The FCI rejects a once-repeated theory that it originated from Greyhound–Borzoi crosses; the chronology does not fit.
VBO:0201032.historicalRoots: Polish hunting sighthound documented since the medieval period.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 333: Polish Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard cites thirteenth-century Polish records, robust build and rejects the Borzoi-cross origin theory.

VBO:0201048.summary: The Poodle’s elegant clips can hide an older job in wildfowling and water. Its dense curly coat and agile frame came through French breeding from Barbet-related stock; the FCI recognizes four size varieties, from toy to standard.
VBO:0201048.interestingFact: The French name caniche is linked to cane, the word for a female duck.
VBO:0201048.historicalRoots: French waterfowl dog of Barbet-related ancestry, later a companion in four sizes.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 172: Poodle
sources.evidence: FCI standard explains wildfowling, Barbet relationship, caniche etymology, curly coat and four sizes.

VBO:0201071.summary: The Portuguese Sheepdog, or Cão da Serra de Aires, worked the Alentejo plains moving and watching sheep, cattle, goats, horses and pigs. Its long, shaggy coat and hardy, medium-sized frame suit a dog selected for distance and sharp changes in temperature.
VBO:0201071.interestingFact: The standard names five kinds of livestock in its traditional working brief.
VBO:0201071.historicalRoots: Alentejo all-purpose livestock herder and watcher.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 93: Portuguese Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Alentejo region, five livestock types, endurance, temperature variation and shaggy coat.

VBO:0201089.summary: The Pug has Chinese roots and a long history as a compact companion, later reaching Europe through Dutch trading networks. Its square body, curled tail, short coat and dark mask make a distinctive outline, with open nostrils and non-protruding eyes part of its functional form.
VBO:0201089.interestingFact: The FCI says open nostrils and eyes that do not protrude are part of correct breed type.
VBO:0201089.historicalRoots: Chinese companion dog spread to Europe through Dutch trade.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 253: Pug
sources.evidence: FCI standard covers China, Dutch East India Company route, square build, curled tail, mask and functional nostril/eye requirements.

VBO:0000670.summary: The Pyrenean Mastiff is a very large Spanish mountain guardian once used against wolves and bears around livestock. Its strong, balanced frame, thick coat and prominent head were meant for protection without sacrificing the movement needed to travel with flocks.
VBO:0000670.interestingFact: The standard explicitly warns that great size should not make the dog look sluggish.
VBO:0000670.historicalRoots: Spanish Pyrenean livestock guardian against large predators.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 92: Pyrenean Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI standard states predator-defense use, very large size, thick coat, balanced frame and avoidance of sluggishness.

VBO:0201132.summary: The Redbone Coonhound is an American scent hound bred to trail and tree raccoons. It carries a smooth, rich red coat, long ears and an athletic outline; selective breeding gradually replaced the black saddle markings seen on many early dogs.
VBO:0201132.interestingFact: George F. L. Birdsong’s Georgia hounds were important foundation stock for the modern breed.
VBO:0201132.historicalRoots: U.S. raccoon-trailing and treeing hound with Georgia foundation lines.

sources.title: UKC Redbone Coonhound breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard describes Georgia foundation stock, raccoon work, early black saddles, solid-red selection and hound build.

VBO:0201143.summary: The Rottweiler takes its name from the German town of Rottweil, where cattle driving and guarding became central to its work. Its broad, powerful frame and sharply defined black-and-tan coat still suggest a practical drover, later employed in draft and police roles.
VBO:0201143.interestingFact: The old “Rottweil butcher’s dog” could guard cattle and property and also pull loads.
VBO:0201143.historicalRoots: German cattle drover and guard dog associated with Rottweil.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 147: Rottweiler
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Rottweil name, butcher use, droving, guarding, draft and police work; appearance describes powerful black-and-tan build.

VBO:0201180.summary: The Šarplaninac is a mountain livestock guardian associated with the Šar range of the Balkans. A long, coarse coat, substantial bone and steady, ground-covering frame suit long outdoor watches over cattle herds rather than fast pursuit.
VBO:0201180.interestingFact: The FCI standard lists both North Macedonia and Serbia in the breed’s official origin.
VBO:0201180.historicalRoots: Balkan livestock guardian of the Šar mountain region.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 41: Sarplaninac
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Serbia/Macedonia origin, Šar mountain name, cattle-herd protection, long coarse coat and robust mountain-dog build.

VBO:0201185.summary: The Schnauzer is the medium-sized German stable dog once called a rough-haired Pinscher. Its square body, wiry coat, strong eyebrows and beard give the familiar outline; horses and a knack for catching rodents shaped its early farmyard role.
VBO:0201185.interestingFact: The breed was known as a “Rattler” before the Schnauzer name took hold.
VBO:0201185.historicalRoots: Southern German stable and rodent-control dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 182: Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes southern German stable use, rodent-catching nickname, 1895 rough-haired Pinscher designation and wiry square form.

VBO:0201200.summary: The Sealyham Terrier is a small but substantial Welsh working terrier, longer than it is tall, with a weather-resistant white coat and strong jaws. Its compact build recalls earth work even though the modern dog is often encountered as a companion.
VBO:0201200.interestingFact: The official outline is oblong rather than square, despite its short legs.
VBO:0201200.historicalRoots: Welsh earth-working terrier later kept as a companion.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 74: Sealyham Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies terrier use, oblong substantial build, strong jaws and predominantly white weather-resistant coat.

sources.title: AKC: Sealyham Terrier history
sources.evidence: Locates development at Sealy Ham in Wales and traces vermin and earth-working origin.

VBO:0201223.summary: The Shih Tzu’s roots lie in Tibet, but the breed developed in Chinese imperial palaces before reaching Britain in the 1930s. A long coat and hair rising over the nose create its distinctive “chrysanthemum” face on a sturdy small companion.
VBO:0201223.interestingFact: Britain first recorded imports in 1931 and gave the Shih Tzu a separate register in 1940.
VBO:0201223.historicalRoots: Tibetan roots and Chinese palace development as a companion dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 208: Shih Tzu
sources.evidence: FCI standard distinguishes Tibetan roots from Chinese development, dates British imports and register, and explains chrysanthemum face.

VBO:0201237.summary: The Silky Terrier is an Australian toy terrier developed from Australian and Yorkshire terrier lines. Its small, sturdy frame carries a fine blue-and-tan coat that falls straight and glossy, combining a polished look with unmistakable terrier ancestry.
VBO:0201237.interestingFact: The first breed standard was drawn up in Australia in the early twentieth century.
VBO:0201237.historicalRoots: Australian companion terrier shaped from local and Yorkshire lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 236: Silky Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Australian/Yorkshire ancestry and early standard; appearance describes compact body and silky blue-and-tan coat.

VBO:0201278.summary: The Spanish Mastiff traveled with Spain’s seasonal Merino sheep movements, protecting flocks from wolves and other predators. Its immense body, thick loose skin and dense coat suit an animal bred to stay with livestock across varied routes and pastures.
VBO:0201278.interestingFact: Its working history is tied to the medieval Mesta association of transhumant sheep breeders.
VBO:0201278.historicalRoots: Spanish transhumant flock guardian, especially with Merino sheep.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 91: Spanish Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI standard links Merino migrations and the Mesta to predator defense; appearance describes very large substantial build and dense coat.

VBO:0201315.summary: The Swedish Lapphund is a dark-coated Nordic spitz long associated with the Sámi communities of northern Scandinavia. It served in reindeer herding, hunting and watch work; an upright-eared, curled-tailed silhouette remains central to its identity.
VBO:0201315.interestingFact: The FCI describes it today chiefly as a versatile companion, after centuries of northern working use.
VBO:0201315.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding, hunting and watch dog of Sweden.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 135: Swedish Lapphund
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Sámi-associated reindeer work, hunting and watch use, present companionship and dark spitz appearance.

VBO:0201342.summary: The Tenterfield Terrier is a small Australian terrier with a smooth coat, alert ears and a balanced, athletic frame. Descended from working terriers brought by English settlers, it was valued on farms and around homesteads for controlling rats and other vermin.
VBO:0201342.interestingFact: A natural bobtail occurs in the breed; Dogs Australia describes it as a distinctive Tenterfield feature.
VBO:0201342.historicalRoots: Australian farm and homestead vermin-control terrier.

sources.title: National Tenterfield Terrier Council of Australia: Breed facts
sources.evidence: National breed council traces early English terrier roots, ratting work, small agile build, smooth coat and natural bobtail.

VBO:0201352.summary: The Tibetan Spaniel is a small, slightly long-bodied companion dog from Tibet. Its silky coat, plumed tail and alert expression give a compact but poised outline; despite the name, it belongs to the Tibetan companion-dog tradition rather than the field spaniels.
VBO:0201352.interestingFact: Its FCI classification is among Tibetan companion breeds, not hunting spaniels.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 231: Tibetan Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard lists Tibetan origin and companion classification, slightly long outline, silky coat and plumed tail.

VBO:0201361.summary: The Toy Fox Terrier is a distinctly American miniature of the Smooth Fox Terrier tradition. A sleek, mostly white coat and lithe square body sit on toy scale, while its early usefulness as a barnyard ratter kept the breed’s working-terrier character visible.
VBO:0201361.interestingFact: AKC history records small Smooth Fox Terriers working on American farms before the breed was stabilized.
VBO:0201361.historicalRoots: American small farm ratter developed from Smooth Fox Terrier stock.

sources.title: AKC Toy Fox Terrier official standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard describes toy scale, square athletic body and glossy white coat; AKC breed history records U.S. farm ratting and Smooth Fox Terrier roots.

sources.title: AKC Toy Fox Terrier history
sources.evidence: Confirms related breed variety or history described in the summary.

VBO:0201390.summary: The Volpino Italiano is a small Italian spitz with a dense stand-off coat, pointed ears and a plume curling over its back. Long kept by both wealthy households and ordinary workers, it served as a bright little watchdog as well as a companion.
VBO:0201390.interestingFact: The FCI history notes a Volpino in a Venetian painting by Vittore Carpaccio dated 1502.
VBO:0201390.historicalRoots: Italian household watchdog and companion with European spitz roots.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 195: Volpino Italiano
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Italian spitz ancestry, all-class household history, 1502 painting and characteristic coat/ears/tail.

VBO:0201412.summary: The Welsh Terrier is a compact black-and-tan working terrier with a tight wiry coat. It was used in Wales to hunt fox, badger and otter, leaving a strong, practical outline beneath the tidy beard and lively expression.
VBO:0201412.interestingFact: The breed may share older Celtic roots with the similar-looking Lakeland Terrier, though the standard treats that link as a possibility.
VBO:0201412.historicalRoots: Welsh fox, badger and otter working terrier.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 78: Welsh Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard names traditional quarry, black-and-tan wire coat and possible shared older ancestry with Lakeland Terrier.

VBO:0201423.summary: The White Swiss Shepherd Dog grew from white shepherd lines maintained in North America and then established in Switzerland from the 1970s. Its upright ears, white double coat and balanced herding-dog frame combine a familiar shepherd outline with a distinct Swiss breed history.
VBO:0201423.interestingFact: A male named Lobo, born in 1966, is cited as a progenitor of the Swiss population.
VBO:0201423.historicalRoots: North American white shepherd ancestry established as a Swiss breed.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 347: White Swiss Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard details U.S./Canada lines, 1970s Swiss imports, Lobo and white shepherd appearance.

VBO:0201428.summary: The Wirehaired Vizsla is a Hungarian pointing dog created in the 1930s by crossing the shorthaired Vizsla with the German Wirehaired Pointer. It retained the field role and golden-rust coloring of the Vizsla while adding a harsh coat, brows and beard for a rougher outline.
VBO:0201428.interestingFact: The wire coat marks a comparatively recent branch of the older Hungarian Vizsla tradition.
VBO:0201428.historicalRoots: Hungarian versatile pointing dog created in the 1930s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 239: Wirehaired Vizsla
sources.evidence: FCI standard states the founding cross and decade, pointing use, rust coat and wiry furnishings.

VBO:0201448.summary: The Yorkshire Terrier came from the same nineteenth-century English region as the much larger Airedale. Beneath its long blue-and-tan silk coat sits a small terrier once valued for pursuing rodents; the present breed name was accepted in 1870.
VBO:0201448.interestingFact: Its early ancestry included the old Black and Tan Terrier, with Maltese and Skye Terrier influence also noted by the FCI.
VBO:0201448.historicalRoots: Yorkshire terrier developed in the mid-nineteenth century from several small terrier lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 86: Yorkshire Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard dates Yorkshire origin and 1870 name, describes ancestry and rodent-hunting instinct, and specifies silky blue-and-tan coat.
